item.title: McNabney’s late double powers Ireland to dominant win against Australia
item.description: 3rd v 3rd: Ireland 38-14 Australia Henshaw, Timoney and Baloucoune also scored tries Ireland’s class told in the end. Back-to-back victories to end the year would have been a tonic for a much-criticised Wallabies team and while they started strongly, they were ultimately outclassed. Australia have now lost seven matches in a row against Ireland. There was a time not so long ago when such a statistic would have been unimaginable: it is one of many that demonstrates how Australia have declined as a global force. Sam Prendergast kicked brilliantly, off the tee and from hand, to orchestrate a success that was a classic Irish blend of power and finesse. The Ireland fly-half kicked five conversions and a penalty for 13 points and his tactical kicking was world class, too. Two victories against the Wallabies have been achieved in the Nations Championship, and this was more convincing than the 33-31 ten-try thriller in Sydney in July. Continue reading...

item.title: Texas rock shelter yields 6,500-year-old kit with boomerang, darts and hide
item.description: In a remarkable archaeological find in West Texas, researchers uncovered a hunting kit that dates back approximately 6,000 years. The collection features various stone and wooden foreshafts, along with essential hunting tools, including a partial atlatl, which is an ancient spear-throwing apparatus. The diversity of materials suggests varying time periods, unlocking valuable insights into the lifestyles and surroundings of these ancient communities.

item.title: The explosion of extreme wealth is the major problem of our time | Bernie Sanders
item.description: At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class We are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class. Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.” Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. item.title: The US army just detonated a poison bomb over Iowa | Steven Donziger
item.description: The shocking situation in Iowa is a metaphor for much of what is wrong with the United States There’s no way to hide it: the US government just deliberately detonated a poison bomb of lead azide over the state of Iowa when a totally safe alternative was available. The problem in Iowa was relatively simple to solve. The army for decades had stored lead underground at a munitions facility. As far back as 2009, the government knew the lead was deteriorating and might blow up on its own. But it procrastinated. Finally, in March, the army hired a Georgia-based company to use a chemical spray to neutralize the lead, creating a non-hazardous byproduct that can be disposed of in landfills. This may be an opportune moment to snap up pre-Christmas bargains on the high street but Maro Itoje and his side are rather more intent on securing a priceless little chunk of history. Never before in 121 years have England’s men beaten New Zealand in three consecutive Tests and the last time their opponents lost six times in a calendar year was back in 1949. item.description: After eight years of socialist-led government, Spain is at a crossroads. Can Pedro Sánchez pull off another electoral comeback, or will the conservative Partido Popular make way for the far right into national government for the first time since the end of Franco's 40-year brutal reign? Just back from Madrid, Richard Werly, Europe correspondent for the Swiss daily Blick, joins Angela Diffley to examine the final days of campaigning and the generational divisions shaping Sunday’s snap elections. The youth are divided between the left and the far-right Vox party. Sánchez, nicknamed the “Teflon politician”, has campaigned heavily on housing and social issues. “We may see an outgoing prime minister performing better than expected,” says Werly.

item.description: To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law. item.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
item.description: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any hum

item.title: The Guardian view on the Children’s Booker prize: everyone is a winner | Editorial
item.description: In a landscape dominated by the same names and celebrity authors, this new award shines a spotlight on great titles that might have been overlooked “Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” asked Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the former children’s laureate and chair of the inaugural Children’s Booker prize , as the shortlist was announced this week. In nearly 60 years of the adult prize, the only children’s book to have made the longlist is Philip Pullman’s The Amber Spyglass in 2001. Now children’s fiction has its own Booker, with four of the seven judges aged between eight and 12. Crucially, the kids get the casting vote. The shortlist, “the great eight”, includes five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Big names such as Eoin Colfer, Liz Hyder and Shaun Tan appear alongside less established writers. There is time travel, humour and sci-fi fantasy, in novels dealing with war, grief and identity. item.title: Veruschka obituary
item.description: German model and artist whose bold and dynamic shoots made her one of the biggest stars of 1960s fashion The aspiring model Vera von Lehndorff created “Veruschka” – little Vera – as a memorable alternative persona whose existence was performance art. She used her natural resources: a 6ft-plus-tall body that, horizontal, could fill an entire glossy magazine spread; a face with magnificent bone architecture and feline eyes; and a long mane that was amenable to brutal short cuts and extraordinary coiffures. All were animated by her instinct for making shapes in air – not a model’s poses but a dancer’s movements that only a click of the lens could catch. Watch her seducing the camera of the photographer, played by David Hemmings , in Michelangelo Antonioni ’s 1966 film Blow Up to see her original act in action. Continue reading...

item.description: After a 12-year run, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s last episode of Chicken Shop Date – a therapy session with Esther Perel – is being shown in cinemas. It’s a fittingly grand finale for a YouTube cult favourite that far outgrew its medium The decision to screen the full final series of Chicken Shop Date in cinemas before the finale airs on YouTube is, it could be argued, overkill. The cinema is a place where you sit rapt among like-minded people, bombarded with cutting-edge sound design and world-class visuals. On the other hand, the fun interview show that is Chicken Shop Date is the thing I watch alone on my computer while I pick my toenails. It isn’t a natural fit, is what I’m trying to say. And yet, goddamn it if the whole thing didn’t leave me slightly choked up. He recounts a police intervention last October and the case of a student facing trial for defending a classmate, and has the full support of several teachers. item.title: They crossed the doom loop of Groundhog Day with Nightmare on Elm Street. Voilà – it’s Peter Mandelson | Robert Hutton
item.description: He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works? What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays. But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name

item.title: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA
item.description: Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer . The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradict a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weedkiller is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup’s producer, Bayer. The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generate new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations. Continue reading...

She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle , named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen . It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night. Almost a century later, arts and culture have replaced cars as the great urban consumables of our age. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. item.title: ‘I am scared’: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order - and why it’s time to speak out against big tech
item.description: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she talks about corporate lawfare, and the growing backlash against NDAs George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns. The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.” Continue reading...

Having defied her parents’ wishes to leave the country age 18 and commence her musical journey, she travelled through Transylvania’s remote villages to learn doine (songs) and strigături (traditional rhymed shouts/calls), and named her album after a song taught to her by farmer Maria Dulău, a woman awarded a title to aim for by the Romanian National Institute of Heritage: Living Human Treasure. “Dorul” is like the Welsh hiraeth or Galician saudade , referencing longing and homesickness, and “trece” explains how these feelings travel, wander and pass. item.description: They weathered excess, illness and being dropped and defrauded, but Echobelly are happily back as a duo. But Sonya Madan remembers it differently. Her band Echobelly were also touring the US that year, and the two groups hung out backstage at each other’s gigs. “I’m gonna blow a myth!” she hoots. “For me, half the stuff about Oasis was made up by their press people. The people around them were partying; everyone was, including us, but it wasn’t that much. Liam was such a sweetheart, I used to go drinking with Noel, we were all mates.” Continue reading...

item.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
item.description: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how w

Finally, Leigh had a brilliant idea. Why not put on Topsy-Turvy, his 1999 costume romp about the making of The Mikado? Problem solved, perfect choice. “It’s not like a habit,” he says hurriedly. “I don’t sit there watching my films every night like Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard. item.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
item.description: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets. Continue reading...

item.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
item.description: Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found. The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991. Continue reading...

item.description: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. item.title: Premier League’s burst of early sendings-off may not last – but red cards are on the rise for a reason
item.description: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early. The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. item.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

item.description: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, four months before the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to victory at the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentinos Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 Reconstruction of radiative forcing resulting from worldwide peatland drainage over the past two centuries reveals a persistent net warming effect caused by the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions over that of avoided CH4 emissions.

item.title: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11275-z A multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human coronary artery disease provides a framework for mapping disease-associated genetic variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

item.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11301-0 Architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer drive cell state diversification through mechanochemical reprogramming of stem cell identities.

item.title: A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11315-8 In flies, sugar-sensing enteric neurons activate brain neurons that inhibit crop duct motor neurons, relaxing the foregut muscles to facilitate food transfer to the crop, which sustains ingestion and regulates food intake.

item.title: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11353-2 Quantum confocal microscopy enables deterministic preparation of high-photon-number Fock-like states with up to 500 photons, reducing photon-number variance by 21.5 dB and achieving record displacement-sensing precision 19.2 dB beyond the standard quantum limit.

item.title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11287-9 RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) is enhanced by redesigned TnsA and a holo complex whose coordinated conformational licensing reveals a conserved mechanistic framework for engineering highly active CASTs.

item.title: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11341-6 Dental morphology and proteomic analyses of fossils from southern China identify lineages with and without Denisovan affinity, indicating the diversity of hominin populations in this region in the Middle to Late Pleistocene.

item.title: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11313-w Sustainable cement production can be achieved by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds.

item.title: Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11318-5 Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features.

item.title: Augmenting reality with integrated photonics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11146-7 Integrated photonics could overcome key size, power and performance trade-offs in augmented-reality glasses, enabling compact, efficient displays while opening opportunities across quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

item.title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11304-x An enzymatic method for making high-molecular-weight polysaccharides in a way similar to synthetic polymerization techniques, rather than biosynthetically, is presented.

item.title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11309-6 Coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor man’s Majoranas are demonstrated in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains, providing a foundation for topologically protected qubits in longer chains.

item.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11311-y Interrogation of the clustered protocadherin locus shows an unexpected ability of genes to transcribe within a seemingly silent chromatin environment.

item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11196-x Structural analyses reveal the mechanism underlying RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) and provide a framework for developing CASTs into site-specific genome-editing tools.

item.title: Clinical landscape of cardiometabolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11231-x This Review covers the current state of research into heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) from a variety of perspectives, focusing on the clinical context.

item.title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11151-w The use of an extremophile fungus-derived gene decouples the trade-off of drought stress and reduced crop yield by boosting drought resilience and increasing yields in wheat, rice and maize.

item.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11354-1 Climate change and natural disturbances are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics: warming tends to shift tree abundance upslope whereas major disturbances, such as wildfires and insect outbreaks, tend to shift it downslope, creating opposing pressures on tree species’ elevational redistribution.

item.title: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11288-8 Niobium phosphide semimetal nanoribbons show decreasing resistivity with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects via industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication.

item.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11338-1 The artificial intelligence platform ORIDTP enabled de novo design of potent dual-target therapeutic peptides, generating candidate anti-obesity, antidiabetic and anticancer peptides with strong in vivo efficacy and broad cross-target generalizability.

item.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11326-5 A high-throughput synthetic embryology platform reveals how transient spatial cues establish two self-sustaining signalling centres that organize trunk-like morphogenesis, enabling the study of early human development and congenital disorders.

item.title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

item.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11279-9 A phototransport regime driven by spin exchange is demonstrated in manganese-doped quantum dot solids, enabling the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers and yielding submillimetre drift lengths.

item.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

item.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease

item.description: Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one. Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. Continue reading...

And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
